title: Knowledge check: Profiling and Benchmarking

questions.prompt: For “Profiling and Benchmarking”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: Profiling and Benchmarking is one step in Advanced R Programming and Performance; advanced behavior is best understood by observing semantics and measuring bottlenecks, not guessing. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Profiling and Benchmarking” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Measuring Runtime” as part of lesson 227. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Profiling and Benchmarking” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Prefer clarity first; profile representative data before optimizing and verify optimized results against a reference. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
